note: This-not-that: everyday decisions, ingredients first. The single source of truth for the app (asset), the public pages (/swaps/<id>/) and the machine-readable copy (/swaps.json). Hand-written, cited, dated. No ranking exists; the pick is a trait, not a brand. The link slot stays empty until a named product has been verified by a person.

swaps.title: Laundry and dishwasher detergent
swaps.question: Is what goes down your drain river-safe?

avoid.why: Phosphorus is fertilizer. Down a drain it feeds algae faster than a river can breathe; the bloom dies, rots, and takes the oxygen with it.
They do not clean anything. They make white look whiter under light, and they are slow to break down once they leave the machine.

prefer.why: The one word that matters, and it is a claim a label can be held to.
Less that has to be broken down downstream, and less on your skin.

prefer.trait: a full drum and a cold wash
prefer.why: Half the swap is how much you use, not which bottle. Cold and full is already an action on the shelf.

pick.label: Any detergent that says phosphate-free on the front
pick.note: Brands change their recipes; the word on the front is the thing to trust. Check dishwasher tablets especially: in much of the world laundry powder went phosphate-free by law, tablets did not always follow.

nearby.label: Use half the dose you use now
nearby.why: Most machines are over-dosed. Halving it is a swap that costs nothing and is already most of the way there.

consequence.line: What feeds the algae starves the river. The frog breathes through her skin, so the water is her air.

sources.title: Regulation (EU) No 259/2012 on phosphates in consumer laundry and dishwasher detergents
sources.what: limits phosphorus to 0.5 g per laundry wash (2013) and 0.3 g per dishwasher wash (2017) because of eutrophication

sources.title: Environment Committee calls for laundry and dishwasher detergent phosphate ban
sources.what: phosphates released into water cause algae to grow at the expense of other aquatic life

swaps.title: What you put on the garden
swaps.question: Who else eats what you spray?

avoid.why: The slug eats the pellet, the hedgehog eats the slug. Banned for outdoor use in the UK in 2022 for exactly that reason: birds, toads and hedgehogs were dying second-hand.

A systemic insecticide is in the whole plant, pollen included. The EU banned outdoor use of the main three in 2018 for the bees; the same molecules are still sold for gardens in much of the world, imidacloprid most of all.

prefer.trait: nothing, and a slightly untidy garden
prefer.why: A hedgehog and a thrush are slug control. They need somewhere to sleep and something to eat, which is the untidy corner.

prefer.trait: ferric phosphate pellets, if you must
prefer.why: Slugs stop feeding; the predators that eat the slugs are not poisoned in turn. Less effective, and that is the trade.

prefer.trait: hand-picking at dusk, with a torch
prefer.why: Ten minutes, no chemistry, and you meet the night shift of your own garden.

pick.label: No sprays, no pellets, one untidy corner left for the helpers
pick.note: This is the one card where the best product is no product. If you buy anything, buy the ferric phosphate kind and read the active ingredient, not the front.

nearby.label: Spray only at dusk, and never on anything in flower
nearby.why: If you cannot go without, the bees are home by dusk and the flowers are where they feed. It is a smaller change that removes most of the harm.

consequence.line: The hedgehog eats the slug that ate the pellet. Poison climbs the food chain one meal at a time.

sources.title: Metaldehyde slug pellets banned in the UK
sources.what: outdoor sale and use banned from 1 April 2022 following advice on risks to birds, toads and hedgehogs; ferric phosphate named as the alternative

sources.title: Metaldehyde slug pellets to be banned from spring 2022
sources.what: the decision was taken to better protect wildlife; harm through direct ingestion or contaminated molluscs

sources.title: An overview of agricultural neonicotinoid regulation in the EU, Canada, and the United States
sources.what: full outdoor ban on imidacloprid, clothianidin and thiamethoxam in the EU in 2018; thiacloprid withdrawn 2020

sources.title: EPA Actions to Protect Pollinators
sources.what: label language advising homeowners not to use neonicotinoid products; residential turf spray uses of imidacloprid cancelled

avoid.ingredient: the shine that stops you looking
avoid.why: An apple grows its own wax. After washing, packers add a coat so it shines and keeps. The coating itself is food-grade; the trouble is what it seals in. Sprays applied before the coat are harder to wash off after it, and a rinse under the tap barely moves them.

prefer.trait: a baking soda soak: about two teaspoons in a litre of water, 12 to 15 minutes
prefer.why: The measured method. In a 2017 study, surface residues of two common orchard pesticides were gone after 12 to 15 minutes in a one percent baking soda solution; tap water and bleach did not manage it.
An apple that did not travel far did not need a coat to survive the trip.

prefer.trait: organic when it is the one fruit you buy most
prefer.why: Apples are among the most sprayed fruits. If you change one thing, change the one you eat every day.

pick.label: The dull one, soaked in baking soda water
pick.note: Shine is a sales decision, not a freshness one. Choose by feel and smell, then soak. If the label says waxed, the soak matters more, not less.

nearby.label: Peel it
nearby.why: Loses fibre and the best of the flavour, but takes the coat and the surface residue with it. An honest second best.

consequence.line: Every apple exists because a bee visited the blossom. What is sprayed on the tree is sprayed on her.

sources.title: Effectiveness of Commercial and Homemade Washing Agents in Removing Pesticide Residues on and in Apples
